History of Present Illness:
Mrs Doe is a 72-year-old female with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type II diabetes mellitus who presented to the emergency department with complaints of chest pain and shortness of breath. She reports experiencing chest pain radiating to her arms and jaw, worse with deep inspiration, starting 30 minutes prior to arrival. The pain was described as crushing in nature and rated 8/10 in severity. She also reports feeling anxious and lightheaded upon standing up. She has never experienced symptoms like these before. Her medical history includes coronary artery disease with previous myocardial infarction 5 years ago, atrial fibrillation, and chronic kidney disease stage III.

Physical Exam:
Vital signs: Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, pulse 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. General appearance: Mrs Doe appears uncomfortable and anxious. Head and neck exam shows jugular venous distension. Cardiovascular exam reveals a regular rhythm with tachycardia. Pulmonary exam shows bilateral lung fields clear to auscultation, but decreased breath sounds over the left lower lobe. Abdominal exam reveals a soft abdomen without tenderness. Extremities show normal capillary refill.

Pertinent Results:
EKG: sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST segment changes. Troponins elevated at 0.45 ng/mL. Echo: EF 40%, moderate mitral regurgitation.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mrs Doe underwent cardiac catheterization showing critical stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery treated with angioplasty and stenting. She remained hemodynamically unstable post-procedure requiring vasopressors and inotropes. She was subsequently stabilized and placed on telemetry monitoring. Throughout her stay, she received antibiotics and anticoagulation therapy.

Discharge Medications:
Aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50mg twice daily, simvastatin 20mg daily, furosemide 20mg daily, spironolactone 25mg daily, warfarin 5mg daily.

Discharge Instructions:
Follow-up appointment scheduled with cardiology clinic in 2 weeks. Continue all medications as directed by your cardiologist. Monitor for signs of bleeding or infection. Limit physical activity to avoid strain on heart. Schedule follow-up echocardiogram in 3 months.
